st-elizabeth-church-roses-square.description: The Roman Catholic parish church of St Elizabeth of Hungary stands on Rózsák tere in Erzsébetváros. Designed by Imre Steindl, the architect of the Hungarian Parliament, it has two 76-metre neo-Gothic towers, a richly furnished interior and a statue of the saint in front, from which the Square of Roses takes its name.
paragraphs: St Elizabeth's Church stands on Rózsák tere, the Square of Roses, in Budapest's seventh district, Erzsébetváros. It is a Roman Catholic parish church, and the parish gives its address as Rózsák tere 8. Its two towers, each 76 metres high according to Visit Hungary, make it easy to spot above the surrounding streets.

The building exists because the first church was too small. The independent parish of Erzsébetváros was founded in 1881 and built a modest eclectic church to plans by Győző Czigler, but the district grew quickly. A building committee was formed in 1889, and on 28 July 1892 the neo-Gothic design of Imre Steindl was accepted. Steindl is best known for the Hungarian Parliament Building, and Visit Hungary notes that visitors can see similarities between the façades of the two buildings.

Construction began in September 1893. King Franz Joseph I laid the foundation stone in person on 20 October 1895, and the church was consecrated on Ascension Thursday, 16 May 1901. Visit Hungary gives the floor area as 1,800 square metres and the capacity as 2,560 people, which explains why the church feels so large for an ordinary parish.

Inside, the furnishings were mostly made by well-known Hungarian craftsmen. Visit Hungary lists the main altar, the pulpit, the baptismal font, a Wedding Altar, the Altar of Archangel Gabriel, a Requiem Altar and an altar of St Anthony of Padua. Bombs hit the church in the Second World War; the parish says the damage was repaired by 1949, and a full renovation of the exterior and interior ran from 1995, with the exterior finished by 2004 and the interior by 2007.

In front of the church stands a statue of St Elizabeth by József Damkó, placed there in 1932 on the 700th anniversary of the saint's death. The square is named after the roses that are her traditional attribute. Visit Hungary dates the statue and the renaming to 1931, so sources differ by a year. On 29 April 2023 Pope Francis met poor people, refugees and charity representatives in the church during his visit to Hungary.
tips: This is an active parish church. Check the parish website, rozsaktere.hu, or ask the parish for Mass times and when visitors can enter the church.
Look at the façade and towers from the square and compare them with the Hungarian Parliament, also by Imre Steindl.
Read the story of the roses before you go: Visit Hungary explains the tradition that gave the square its name.
Remember that the first, smaller church of the parish still exists as a separate building, now used by the Greek Catholic Church.

st-anne-church-batthyany-square.description: St Anne's is the Baroque parish church of Felsővízváros, the upper part of Buda's Víziváros, on Batthyány tér across the Danube from the Parliament. Begun in 1740 and completed in 1761 according to most sources, it is entered by steps down from the square, and the parish is known for its Jehmlich organ.
paragraphs: St Anne's Church is the Roman Catholic parish church of Felsővízváros, Upper Víziváros, at Batthyány tér 7 in Budapest's first district. English Wikipedia places Batthyány Square on the Buda bank directly opposite the Hungarian Parliament Building and describes the church as one of Budapest's most beautiful Baroque buildings. Its dedication is to Saint Anne.

The parish itself is older than the present building. According to the Hungarian Wikipedia article on the parish, it was founded in 1390, destroyed by the Ottomans in 1540 and re-founded in 1687, with baptismal registers starting in 1693. In 1724 the Buda city council bought a property on the site and had it converted into a chapel and parish house with a tower. The Jesuits served the parish, and as the congregation grew, work on a new church began in 1740.

The builder first commissioned was Kristóf Hamon. After his death, Máté Nöpauer of Brno finished the church in 1761, according to the same article. Wikidata records both men as architects and gives 1740 to 1761 as the construction period, while a caption on Wikimedia Commons dates the church to 1762, so the exact completion year varies by source. The Jesuits ran the parish until the order was suppressed in 1773; priests of the Esztergom archdiocese then took over, and in 1787 Archbishop József Batthyány split the parish in two.

A detail worth noticing is the level of the square. A We Love Budapest article on the history of Batthyány tér explains that landfill added in 1870, during the regulation of the Danube, left some older entrances below street level, so you reach St Anne's by going down a staircase rather than up. The same article places the church on the south side of the square, beside the market hall.

Inside, the parish website highlights the church's Jehmlich organ, which it describes as of European renown and recently repaired. The parish also runs a choir. The congregation was mostly German-speaking until the late 18th century, according to the Hungarian Wikipedia article, and the parish remains active today.
tips: St Anne's is a working parish church. Check the parish website, felsovizivaros.plebania.hu, for Mass times and for when visitors can go in.
Look at the steps down from the square: they come from the 1870 landfill described in a We Love Budapest article on the square's history.
Combine the visit with Batthyány tér itself and the view across the Danube to the Parliament.
If you are interested in the organ, the parish site lists music events and concerts.

inner-city-parish-church-assumption.description: The Inner City Parish Church of the Assumption sits at the Pest end of Elisabeth Bridge, which was designed as an arch so the church could stay. A Gothic hall church that served as a mosque under Ottoman rule, it still has a mihrab, and Roman fort remains were found beneath it in 2014 to 2016.
paragraphs: The Inner City Parish Church of the Assumption, in Hungarian the Belvárosi Nagyboldogasszony Főplébánia, stands at Március 15. tér 2 in Budapest's fifth district. It is a Roman Catholic parish church of the Archdiocese of Esztergom-Budapest, and its own website has a section for visitors as well as for parishioners. The parish gives the church's age as more than 950 years, although the date of the first Christian church is unknown.

What you see today is mostly a Gothic hall church with three aisles and an ambulatory, built from around 1370 to 1490 under King Louis the Great and later kings. The south tower dates from the reign of Matthias. Visit Hungary records that Matthias was elected king here in 1458 and Ulászló in 1490, and that the church's earliest layers go back to Roman times: a renovation in 2014 to 2016 uncovered remains of the Roman fort Contra Aquincum.

During Ottoman rule, from 1541, the church was used as a mosque, and a mihrab, the prayer niche, still survives in the wall. After the Ottomans were expelled in 1686 only the Gothic sanctuary was usable. Archbishop György Széchényi paid for a vault and conservation work on the nave in the following decades. The result is a building where Gothic, Ottoman and Baroque elements sit side by side.

The church is closely tied to Pest's public life. Count István Széchenyi lay in state here in 1860, Franz Joseph took the royal oath in front of the church in 1867, though sources differ on whether this was before or after his coronation, and Visit Hungary says Franz Liszt was a frequent guest and occasional conductor between 1858 and 1871. When Elisabeth Bridge was planned in the 1890s, demolishing the church was considered; instead the bridge was designed as an arch so the church could stay.

Look for the sanctuary vault, painted by Imre Steindl in 1889, and the 14th-century Madonna fresco found behind the main altar in 2010. The church was heavily damaged in 1944, losing its high altar and a tower spire; the new spire was finished by 1957. The 2014 to 2016 excavations ended when Cardinal Péter Erdő blessed the church on 14 August 2016. The parish site also mentions lookouts in the Baroque towers, which opened to visitors in 2020.
tips: This is an active parish. The parish website, belvarosiplebania.hu, has the current visiting arrangements, Mass times, tower lookout information and a virtual tour.
Groups should register in advance with the parish, which lists a separate contact for guided visits.
Stand on the bridge side and look at how Elisabeth Bridge curves around the church, which the Visit Hungary history describes as deliberate.
Look for the mihrab inside, a reminder of the Ottoman period.

deak-square-lutheran-church.description: A plain neoclassical Lutheran church at Deák Ferenc tér 4, designed by Mihály Pollack and built between 1799 and 1808, with a Doric-pilastered façade rebuilt by József Hild in 1856. It is an active Lutheran parish church and stands next to the Evangelical National Museum.
paragraphs: The Deák Square Lutheran Church, in Hungarian the Deák téri evangélikus templom, stands at Deák Ferenc tér 4 in Budapest's fifth district. It is a Lutheran, or Evangelical, parish church and still hosts services and concerts. A We Love Budapest listing calls it the city's oldest and largest Protestant church, and notes that the Evangelical National Museum operates next to it.

The architect was Mihály Pollack, one of the main builders of neoclassical Pest. A We Love Budapest article on Pollack says he designed the church in the late 1790s with master builder János Krausz and took over the project after Krausz died. Hungarian Wikipedia gives the construction period as 1799 to 1808. The building was not used as a church at once: from July 1809 to spring 1811 it served as a military clothing store, and it was consecrated at Pentecost in 1811.

The exterior is deliberately plain. The façade has four Doric pilasters, a cornice with triglyphs and metopes, and a triangular pediment, under a large convex metal roof. József Hild rebuilt the main façade in 1856. Pollack's design was compact and unadorned, which the We Love Budapest article says sparked debate at a time when late Baroque still shaped architecture.

Inside is a single rectangular nave with a double gallery, completed in 1820. Pollack designed the altar, which carries a painting by Ferenc Lochbichler based on Raphael's Transfiguration, and Lőrinc Dunaiszky made the pulpit and the red marble baptismal font. The church was changed over time: in 1875 the classicist tower was removed for structural reasons and the barrel vault was replaced with a coffered ceiling.

In the courtyard, two bronze reliefs commemorate the 500th anniversary of Luther's birth and the 300th anniversary of Bach's birth. A marble plaque on the façade records that Lajos Kossuth had his sons baptised here. The church also sheltered many people during the great flood of 1838.
tips: This is an active parish church. Check the parish website, deakter.hu, for services, music events and when visitors can enter.
The Evangelical National Museum is next door but is a separate institution; check its own site for opening times and tickets.
Walk around to the courtyard side to see the bronze reliefs of Luther and Bach mentioned in the Hungarian Wikipedia article.
Compare the plain façade with the more ornate churches elsewhere in the city centre.

st-emeric-cistercian-church.description: The Buda Cistercian Saint Emeric Church at Villányi út 25 is a neo-Baroque parish church consecrated in 1938 and designed by Gyula Wälder. Its twin towers face Feneketlen Lake in Szentimreváros, and it stands beside the Cistercian school; the parish has again been run by the order since 1989.
paragraphs: The Buda Cistercian Saint Emeric Church, in Hungarian the Budai ciszterci Szent Imre-templom, stands at Villányi út 25 in Szentimreváros, part of Budapest's eleventh district, Újbuda. It is a Roman Catholic parish church of the Archdiocese of Esztergom-Budapest, dedicated to Saint Emeric, and the parish has again been run by the Cistercians since 1989. The parish office is at Himfy utca 9.

The church was designed by the architect and university professor Gyula Wälder for the Cistercian order. Hungarian Wikipedia gives its style as neo-Baroque and says it was built in 1938, the jubilee year of Saint Emeric, and consecrated that year by Cardinal-Primate Jusztinián Serédi. Wikidata gives the date as 6 November 1938. It belongs to a larger complex: the Cistercians settled in Buda in 1912, and the Feneketlen Lake article says Wälder planned a church, monastery, gymnasium and boarding school near the lake, with construction beginning in 1927.

The site relates closely to the lake. According to Hungarian Wikipedia, Feneketlen Lake began as a clay pit worked for a brickworks, and its origin is usually dated to 1877; the brickworks closed in 1889. When the surrounding park was landscaped in 1958 to 1960, the designer Mihály Mőcsényi aimed to make the church's twin towers visible as a reflection on the water, turning that view into a landmark of the district. The church and the Budai Ciszterci Szent Imre Gimnázium stand on the north side of the lake, across Villányi út.

Hungarian Wikipedia lists a main altar with a painting, a pulpit, side altars, a painted coffered ceiling, porcelain Stations of the Cross, a statue of Mary and a baptismal chapel with the Batthyány-Strattmann baptistery. The interior was renovated in 1972 to 1975 and the exterior in 1976 to 1979, and the façade and roof were reconstructed in 2019 to 2020, when the towers also received clocks. The parish website lists a sanctuary renovation project for 2026.
tips: This is an active parish church. Check the parish website, szentimre.hu, for Mass times, visiting arrangements and the current renovation work on the sanctuary.
Walk to the lake first and look back across the water at the twin towers, the view the park designer planned.
Feneketlen Lake is a short walk away; Hungarian Wikipedia describes the park around it, with an open-air stage, a running track and sculptures.
The church is beside an active Cistercian school, so show consideration for pupils in the surrounding streets.

st-margaret-parish-church-lehel-square.description: The Árpád-házi Szent Margit-templom, popularly the Lehel tér church, is a neo-Romanesque parish church in Újlipótváros designed by István Möller and modelled on the Zsámbék church ruin. Built from 1931 to 1933, it has frescoes by Henrik Heintz and stained glass by Miksa Róth.
paragraphs: The Árpád-házi Szent Margit-templom, the Church of Saint Margaret of the House of Árpád, is popularly known as the Lehel téri templom, the Lehel Square church. It is a Roman Catholic parish church in Budapest's thirteenth district. Hungarian Wikipedia gives its address as Váci út 34, 1132 Budapest, in the Újlipótváros neighbourhood, and says it stands on Szent Margit tér, a small square separated from Lehel tér on 29 May 2019.

The parish grew out of a Chapel Association founded in 1919. A parish community formed in 1920 under Gyula Zaymus, and in 1923 it became an independent parish. The church was built between 1931 and 1933 to plans by István Möller, who based them on the ruins of the church at Zsámbék; the master builder was Ferenc Wihart. It was consecrated on 15 October 1933 by Cardinal-Primate Jusztinián Serédi. The total cost was about one million pengő, which the community paid off through donations.

The style is neo-Romanesque, and Hungarian Wikipedia links the thick walls, square towers and portal to the medieval atmosphere of the Zsámbék model. The interior has frescoes by Henrik Heintz, statues by György Nemes Ősz, and stained glass and a rose window by Miksa Róth. A planned altarpiece by Ferenc Chiovini, St Stephen's Missionary Journey, was never completed.

The church took the name Árpád-házi Szent Margit in 1944, after the canonisation of Margaret; before that it was dedicated to Blessed Margaret. It suffered minor damage in the Second World War and was repaired with donations. In 1975 a new liturgical space was designed by Gyula Bárdos, and from 1988 to 1994 the roof, stained glass and interior painting were renovated.

The church sits at the edge of a busy junction. Hungarian Wikipedia describes the neighbouring Lehel Csarnok market hall, built in 2002 to a design by László Rajk Jr. and nicknamed the Kofahajó, on the site of the old Lehel market. The article on Lehel tér lists the M3 metro, which has a Lehel tér station.
tips: This is a working parish church. Check with the parish for current Mass times and when visitors can enter.
Maps may show the church under either Lehel tér or Szent Margit tér, and the street address is Váci út 34.
Look at the rose window and stained glass by Miksa Róth, and the frescoes by Henrik Heintz.
The Lehel Csarnok market hall next to the church is a short walk away.

st-ladislaus-church-kobanya.description: Ödön Lechner's Kőbánya church mixes Romanesque, Gothic, Renaissance, Baroque, Persian and Hungarian folk motifs. Built from 1894 to 1899 and consecrated in 1900, it has Zsolnay tiles and altars, and among Budapest churches only St Stephen's Basilica is taller than its 83-metre tower.
paragraphs: The Kőbánya Saint Ladislaus Church, in Hungarian the Kőbányai Szent László-templom, stands at Szent László tér 25 in Budapest's tenth district. It is a Roman Catholic parish church, owned by the Kőbánya local government according to Hungarian Wikipedia. The Budapest City Archives describe it as a church by Ödön Lechner, built on the site of a former rowing lake. Lechner's father owned a brick factory on Maglódi Street, and the archive notes that Lechner lived in Kőbánya at the time.

The commission was complicated. According to the City Archives, Lechner received the commission in 1891, and his first design, in an unusual Byzantine style with Eastern ornament, had to be revised at the client's request. A second version was also rejected. A third, eclectic and Secessionist, was approved, but Lechner was removed from the project when he judged the deadline unachievable; about a hundred artists then petitioned that the interior should be by the same architect as the exterior. Hungarian Wikipedia counts the designs differently and says Lechner prepared the final design in September 1893.

Construction ran from 1894 to 1899. The cross was blessed on 12 August 1897, and the faithful took possession of the church on 2 April 1899. It was consecrated in June 1900; Hungarian Wikipedia's text gives 27 June, St Ladislaus's day, while its infobox says 28 June. Lechner's style combines Romanesque, Gothic, Renaissance, Baroque, Persian and Hungarian folk elements. The tower is 83 metres high, and in Budapest only St Stephen's Basilica is taller.

Look for the colourful Zsolnay roof tiles outside and the Zsolnay majolica altars and pulpit inside. One side altar was donated by the brewer Antal Dreher, and the stained glass and mosaics are attributed to the workshop of Miksa Róth. The Second World War damaged the building badly, with the original stained glass destroyed, and the Hussar tower burned in 1957.

A long restoration followed. Hungarian Wikipedia dates the complete renovation to 1974 to 1994, while a We Love Budapest article says major reconstruction began in the 1980s and ended in 2001, so sources differ. A statue of Saint Ladislaus by Károly Antal stands in front of the church.
tips: This is an active parish. Check the parish website, szentlaszlo.net, for Mass times and visiting arrangements before you go.
Kőbánya is away from the central tourist area, so plan your route and travel time in advance with the city's public transport planner.
Look up at the roof tiles and the tower; the Zsolnay ceramics are the church's most distinctive features.
Read the Budapest City Archives article on the church's design history, which explains why Lechner's plans changed.

obuda-synagogue.description: The Óbuda Synagogue at Lajos utca 163 is a neoclassical synagogue consecrated in 1821 and designed by András Landherr. After decades as a warehouse and television studio it was rededicated in 2010 and is again an active Orthodox prayer house maintained by EMIH, a Chabad-linked community.
paragraphs: The Óbuda Synagogue, in Hungarian the Óbudai zsinagóga, stands at Lajos utca 163 in Óbuda, Budapest's third district. Its website calls it the capital's oldest functioning Jewish prayer house, and says it is maintained by the EMIH, the Unified Hungarian Israelite Community. The congregation is Orthodox, and Hungarian Wikipedia says Chief Rabbi Slomó Köves has led it since 2010. It is a living place of worship with a weekly schedule of prayer and study.

Jews resettled in Óbuda in the early 18th century under the protection of the Zichy family. The synagogue's history page says that by 1727 they could hold public worship, and that in 1738 construction began on the first synagogue. A Baroque synagogue by Máté Nöpauer followed in 1767 to 1769, but its walls cracked because of poor foundations and unstable soil. In 1817 the Buda Building Committee chose to rebuild it while keeping most of the walls.

The present building is the result. Hungarian Wikipedia credits András Landherr with the design, work began around 1820, and the synagogue was consecrated on 20 July 1821. It received a new south façade with a columned porch of six Corinthian columns and a tympanum inscribed with a Hebrew verse from 1 Kings. The main hall has 662 fixed seats, 364 for men and 298 for women, and a wooden Torah reading table in the centre surrounded by four Empire-style obelisks.

The 20th century was hard on the building. About 3,000 Óbuda Jews died in the Holocaust, according to Hungarian Wikipedia, and from the 1960s the building was sold and used in turn as a museum, a warehouse and a television studio; Magyar Televízió used it as Studio 5 from 1978. In spring 2010 EMIH took it over, and it was rededicated on 5 September 2010. Restoration work included repainting about 25,000 small Stars of David on the vaults, and the restored synagogue was formally reopened on 12 April 2016.
tips: This is an active synagogue and prayer house. Check obudaizsinagoga.hu for current visiting arrangements, services and events before you go.
Respect the prayer schedule: the site lists daily services and a Shabbat programme, so visits should be arranged around them.
Across the street, at the corner of Lajos utca and Zichy utca, a We Love Budapest article places the oldest house in the third district, now an exhibition space of Budapest Galéria.
Pair the visit with a walk around Óbuda; English Wikipedia says that when the synagogue was built, Óbuda's was the largest Jewish community in Hungary.
